youtube_description:
🔔 The e-waste problem isn’t just growing—it’s outpacing the systems built to collect and recycle devices.

Watch the chart race unfold as global e-waste generation rises from tiny piles in the early 2000s into an ~10+ million tonnes/year reality, while “documented collection + recycling” scales much more slowly—leaving a widening informal/unreported gap.

Chapters:
00:00 2000–2004: The quiet ramp-up
03:10 2005–2009: Smartphones enter the mass market
07:40 2010–2014: E-waste accelerates faster than policy
12:20 2015–2019: Collection systems improve, but not enough
16:50 2020–2025: The pandemic decade and the continued backlog
21:10 Who wins? Which lane grows fastest—and who gets crushed?

📌 What to do:
1) Comment “E-WASTE” if you want a follow-up video on specific countries.
2) If you’re building devices: ask where collection targets live.
3) If you’re a consumer: share how you dispose of old phones.

Sources used for the narrative baselines: UN Global E-waste Monitor / ISWM-style aggregation, ITU reports on e-waste and recycling rates, and global tracking summaries compiled for collection/recovery vs informal handling.

instagram_caption:
🚀 The $100B Question: Who’s catching e-waste—fast enough?

Every year, the world produces more discarded electronics than the planet has patience for. And the chart race is brutal: global e-waste generation doesn’t creep upward—it surges. In 2000, the total was about 0.1 million tonnes. By 2010, it passed ~2.3 million tonnes. Then the curve tightens: 2015 lands around ~4.8 million tonnes, 2019 jumps to ~7.4 million tonnes, and by 2025 we’re at an estimated ~10.8 million tonnes annually.

Now look at the “escape hatch”—documented collection. It rises too, but at a slower pace: from near-zero in the early 2000s to roughly ~1.6 million tonnes by 2015, ~2.7 million tonnes by 2019, and ~4.8 million tonnes by 2025. That gap matters. It’s not just a number on a chart—it’s the difference between controlled processing and devices being handled off the books.

That’s why the story gets dramatic when you watch the informal/unreported lane. Even as documented recycling climbs—from ~0.1 million tonnes in the early 2000s to ~2.2 million tonnes in 2015 and ~6.3 million tonnes by 2025—the informal lane remains large. Generated minus documented means informal handling sits around ~5.0 million tonnes by 2020, and still ~5.9 million tonnes by 2025. In other words: the backlog keeps breathing.

What would change the race? Higher take-back rates, stronger e-waste logistics, and recycling targets that match how fast devices are being replaced.

💬 Question: If you had to pick ONE lever—producer take-back, consumer trade-in systems, or better enforcement—which would actually shrink informal e-waste the fastest?

facebook_caption:
The global e-waste challenge is a race between device replacement and the capacity to collect, sort, and recycle electronics. In this timeline comparison, global e-waste generation rises from ~0.1 million tonnes in 2000 to ~10.8 million tonnes by 2025.

While documented collection grows as well—from near-zero in the early 2000s to ~4.8 million tonnes by 2025—its scale does not fully match the growth in generated waste. Documented recycling/recovery increases from ~0.1 million tonnes to ~6.3 million tonnes over the same period.

The resulting difference shows how much e-waste is effectively handled outside formal systems: the informal/unreported lane stays very large, reaching ~5.9 million tonnes by 2025. The key message is clear: even improvements in recycling rates cannot fully close the gap if collection and processing capacity lag behind the speed of electronics turnover.

threads_caption:
Wait—why is the e-waste pile growing faster than recycling?

In 2000 we generated ~0.1M tonnes of e-waste. By 2010 ~2.3M. By 2019 ~7.4M. And by 2025 it’s about ~10.8M tonnes.

The “caught and processed” lanes (documented collection + documented recycling) go up too—but not as fast. Informal/unreported handling stays massive, around ~5.9M tonnes by 2025.

So the real question: what’s the missing piece—better take-back programs, stronger consumer trade-in, or enforcement?

What would you fix first?
